newsitem.title: BELARUS: Belarus capital faces mass rally over poll crisis.
newsitem.headline: Belarus capital faces mass rally over poll crisis.

text.p: Opponents of Belarus President Alexander Lukashenko, who accuse him of building a dictatorship, are garnering their forces for a mass rally on Saturday in a bid to stop him increasing his power.

"We will not be afraid, we will attend a peaceful rally tomorrow, and we will win!" Yuri Khadyka, deputy head of the Belarussian Popular Front, told a crowd of nationalists, liberals and democrats on Friday.
About 2,000 people squeezed into a hall a few hundred metres (yards) from Lukashenko's office to protest against his plans for a November 7 referendum to broaden his powers.

Speakers also slammed him for sluggish reforms which have led to the International Monetary Fund halting loans to the former Soviet republic of 10 million people, sandwiched between Russia and Poland.
The 42-year-old leader has incensed nationalists by trying to form a closer union with Russia and making derogatory comments about the little-used Belarussian language.

Lukashenko, who swept to power in July 1994 on a platform of fighting corruption, has become increasingly authoritarian, ignoring the constitutional court, suspending trade unions and muzzling the media.
Thousands of mostly young Belarussians have filled the streets of Minsk 10 times this year in protests which have at times turned violent and led to hundreds of arrests.

Saturday's protest will set supporters of Lukashenko, attending a congress to back his referendum, against opponents who want to hold a separate poll on November 24 to abolish the presidency and create a parliamentary democracy.

Lukashenko still enjoys strong support in the provinces as a strong man who will rebuild ties with Russia and fight crime and corruption. His opponents are mostly politicians and young people in the capital and in industrial centres.
Some are already predicting bloodshed on Saturday.

"If the situation on October 19 goes out of control, if mass violations of social order are allowed, then we will employ all our forces to stop them," General Boris Tarletski, head of the city police, was quoted as saying in local media.
Deputies on Friday expressed concern over reports that the police were preparing to take violent action.
They called on members of the power structures to exercise restraint and urged both sides not to use force.
The "Svaboda" opposition newspaper published what it said was an official interior ministry document which described steps being taken to prevent unrest.
"Armed groups of four snipers and 12 machine gunners...are ready to use their weapons on hooligan elements," it read.
But presidential spokesman Vladimir Zametalin told Reuters that the opposition could never have got hold of such a document and described the publication as a provocation.

Lukashenko has called 6,000 people to an "All-Belarus People's Congress" to support referendum amendments which would create a two-chamber assembly partly appointed by him and extend his term by more than two years without elections.

The amendments, criticised by parliament, major political parties and legal experts of the Council of Europe, would also allow him to appoint all court judges, half the constitutional court and half the Central Electoral Committee.
